newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean central bank warns currency speculators.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean central bank warns currency speculators.

text.p: South Korea's central bank on Friday issued a warning to currency speculators driving down the won, saying it would aggressively step in to prevent further losses.
A Bank of Korea official, who asked not to be identified, said the bank believed the won was now undervalued against the U.S. dollar.
"We are ready to intervene with the same intensity as we did in February," the official said.
The won opened on Friday at 879. It has lost 3.9 percent of its value against the dollar so far this year after tumbling by 8.2 percent last year.
The official vowed to hold the line at 880 won.
"If anyone goes long at the 880 level, he will risk losses," he said.
The official's comments immediately pushed the won higher. By midday it was trading at 878.60.
In February, the bank sold huge amounts of dollars to bolster the domestic currency when it reached 887. Intervention over two days pushed the currency up by 33.5 won to 853.50 on February 20.
Since then, the won has slid again, pushed lower by a stubborn trade deficit that is creating demand for dollars.

Soon after the central bank's warning, it offered to sell dollars in the three-month forward market at 893.00 won, dealers said. The forward market is a good indication of where traders believe the currency is heading.
Although a weaker won should help exporters and reduce the trade deficit, the effect has been spoiled because the Japanese yen has fallen even more steeply against the dollar.
Japan is South Korea's main export rival.
Economists say a tumbling won has raised import costs and fuelled inflation. It has also burdened companies with higher overseas debt repayments, eroding profits.
A tightening supply of won has also pushed up domestic interest rates. Benchmark three-year corporate bond yields are now at 12.7 percent, a high for the year.

Rising interest rates have helped prolong a stock market slump. The leading share index has dived by 4.5 percent so far this month, and on Friday slumped further, losing 1.14 percent to 650.37 by midday.
Overshadowing the currency and stock markets is slowing economic growth. The economy is officially predicted to expand by six percent this year against 6.9 percent last year.
Private economic think-tanks have forecast growth this year as low as five percent.
